t: Power Update After K-th Largest Insertion II
o:
We maintain a growing collection of numbers. Each query inserts a value, asks for the $k$-th largest element $x$ of the current collection, and replaces $p$ with $p^x \bmod 10^9+7$. We must report $p$ after every query.

**Example 1:** start with `[2]`, p=4. Query [3,1]: nums becomes [2,3]; the 1st largest is 3; p = 4³ = 64. Query [1,2]: nums = [1,2,3]; the 2nd largest is 2; p = 64² = 4096.

**Example 2:** start with [7,5], p=6. Query [4,3]: nums = [4,5,7]; 3rd largest is 4; p = 6⁴ = 1296. Query [7,2]: nums = [4,5,7,7]; 2nd largest is 7; p = 1296⁷ mod 10⁹+7 = 220296870.

With $n, q \le 2\cdot10^4$ there are at most $4\cdot10^4$ elements total, so even $O(n)$ per insertion works ($\approx 8\cdot10^8$ elementary ops worst case, fine in practice with cheap operations). The only real requirements are: support insert + select k-th largest efficiently, and compute modular exponentiation correctly (values like $p^x$ are astronomically large, so we must exponentiate under the modulus). Note $k$ can equal the current size (asking for the minimum).
k: The answer after each query is just pow(p, kth_largest, 1e9+7); all difficulty lies in maintaining order statistics under insertions.
Coordinate-compressing all initial and inserted values lets a Fenwick tree over counts answer 'k-th largest' via binary-lifting descent in O(log n).
Modular exponentiation is mandatory — p^x can have billions of digits otherwise.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force — Re-sort Every Query
a.i: Keep the array as-is; after each insertion, sort it and directly index the k-th largest element (position size - k in ascending order). Sorting dominates at O(n log n) per query, giving O(q·n log n) overall — about 1.3·10¹⁰ comparisons worst case, which is too slow for strict limits but conceptually trivial and correct.
s: Let x = nums[size - k] (the k-th largest).
Set p = pow(p, x, 10^9+7) by fast modular exponentiation and record it.
a.t: O(q · n log n) — each query sorts the whole array of up to n+q elements.
a.sp: O(n + q) — the stored array plus output.

a.i: Precompute the sorted set of all values that will ever appear (initial nums plus every inserted val). A Fenwick tree stores the count of each compressed value. The k-th largest among n elements is the element of ascending rank n - k + 1, which we locate by descending the Fenwick tree's implicit binary structure (binary lifting) in O(log m). Each query is then O(log m): one point update, one descent, one modular exponentiation.
s: Collect all values from nums and all queries, sort and deduplicate to get vals; map each value to its 1-based index.
Initialize a Fenwick tree of zeros; add 1 for every initial num; set n = |nums|.
For each query [val, k]: point-update +1 at index(val), increment n.
Find the smallest index i whose Fenwick prefix sum reaches rank r = n - k + 1 via binary-lifting descent; x = vals[i - 1].
Compute p = pow(p, x, 10^9+7) with fast exponentiation and append it to the answer.
a.t: O((n + q) log(n + q)) — compression sort once, then each query does an O(log m) update, O(log m) selection descent, and O(log x) modular exponentiation.
a.sp: O(n + q) — the compressed value array and Fenwick tree.

w:
In an interview, start with the brute-force sort to establish correctness quickly, then upgrade to the Fenwick-tree solution — it's the expected optimal answer given the topic tags. Alternatives include a balanced BST / order-statistic tree (same complexity) or a sorted container with binary insertion (O(n) per insert, acceptable here due to small constraints).

Common pitfalls: (1) off-by-one when converting k-th largest to ascending rank — it is exactly size − k + 1, and k may equal the current size (minimum element); (2) forgetting the modulus during exponentiation, or overflowing 64-bit products in C++/Java (use long long / long and take % MOD after every multiply); (3) in JavaScript, plain numbers overflow safe-integer range during squaring, so use BigInt; (4) duplicates must be counted individually — the Fenwick tree stores counts, not presence flags.

Edge cases: single-element arrays, k = 1 (maximum) and k = current size (minimum), repeated inserted values, and p already ≥ MOD (reduce before exponentiating).

Likely follow-ups: deletions as well as insertions (Fenwick handles both trivially), online queries without known future values (switch to a balanced BST or a dynamic segment tree over the value range up to 10⁹), or returning the full history of x rather than p.
